# Spatial Measures: Potential Indicators and Pathways

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
Spatial management encompasses both decision processes surrounding delineation of management units (and how they correspond to stock units) and also as a subset of measures setting, with area-based designations for subsets of fishing activities. The spatial distributions of both fishery resources and fishing fleets are dynamic and responsive to multiple socio-economic and environmental drivers. Two cases were identified for spatial measures implemented by the Council that could be informed by ecosystem indicators: bycatch avoidance and establishing habitat conservation areas. 
:::

*  **Key question: Can real time or projected habitat conditions assist with spatial measures setting?** 
*  **Scope: demo for one species or develop a more general approach/process for all?** 


:::::: {.cols data-latex=""}

::: {.col data-latex="{0.49\textwidth}"}
::: {.ltbluebox data-latex=""}
## What information is used now?

The general process for setting spatial measures can be the same as for all other measures as noted in the Measures Setting 1-pager.  Measures are set in specifications. The process for setting measures can be changed by either FMP amendment or framework action. 

\vspace{1ex}

The seasonal Scup Gear Restricted Areas (GRAs) are spatial measures designed to reduce juvenile scup discards in small mesh fisheries. The GRAs have remained the same for years. They are currently being [re-evaluated](https://ccesuffolk.org/marine/fisheries/scup-gra) using fishing and environmental data as well as industry expertise.

\vspace{1ex}

There are several current examples that use habitat indicators to forecast bycatch potential in near-real time. The recently developed [RHAPcast](https://www.rhapcast.org/index.html) uses species distribution model output and hindcast forecasts of habitat (sea surface temperature) to identify areas that maximize target species encounters while minimizing bycatch species encounters. This tool is similar to the [Turtlewatch](https://oceanwatch.pifsc.noaa.gov/turtlewatch.html) approach in the Pacific.   

\vspace{1ex}

```{r rhapcast, out.width="87%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("onepagers/rhapcast-screencap.png"))
```

\vspace{1ex}

Stock and fishery distribution shifts are also being addressed from a [governance perspective](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/511cdc7fe4b00307a2628ac6/t/68e67a313a977f0b7ec34724/1759935025455/Project+7_IRA-Project-Brief.pdf). Indicators developed for this project may also be useful for developing and evaluating spatial measures. 

:::

## Information sources for indicators

### Potential Indicator Sources

* Observer data bycatch estimates
* Species distribution models and data products, e.g. DisMAP (survey data) and NRHA data explorer
* Spatiotemporal environmental forecasts from ocean model output (e.g. MOM6)
* Fishing effort distributions / footprints
* Effects of Fishing database 
* [State of the Ecosystem](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/new-england-mid-atlantic/ecosystems/state-ecosystem-reports-northeast-us-shelf) and [Risk Assessment](https://www.mafmc.org/s/2_MAB_RiskAssess_2024.pdf) indicators


### Potential Pathways

__Bycatch__   

*  Appropriate spatial indicator information could be provided to fishery participants to help them decide how to avoid bycatch and achieve management objectives for bycatch reduction, and/or the Council could implement spatial measures.
*  Indicators of bycatch magnitude for specific areas could be monitored with respect to thresholds that would trigger spatial measures

\vspace{2ex}

__Establishing habitat conservation areas__  

Once objectives for conservation areas are established, an analysis could:

*  Evaluate area measures with indicators of fishery and species spatial overlap:  
    - Spatial distribution of fishery 
    - Spatial distribution of species 
    - Spatial model 
*  Determine habitat effects of fishing activity (e.g. benthic impact studies) 
*  Simulate relevant system drivers (species distribution shifts, fleet movement constraints, etc.) 
*  Determine what spatial management measures meet objectives with minimal side effects?

## Information gaps 

Spatial distribution of fishing effort may not be available/accessible for all sectors/fleets due to confidentiality. There are often challenges to map fishing fleet effort to specific species, and with mismatches in spatial and temporal scale of management areas and processes. Spatial measures also have implications for future monitoring.  


:::
